#data research
I am researching a federal dataset. Find out everything you can about this dataset, such as who publishes it, under what authority or mandate, its history, its typical users, and its benefits to the public. Be sure your research comprehensively covers each of those perspectives, as well as any others that you discover or seem useful. I believe this is accurate information, but please check:

Dataset title: Survey of Consumer Finances (SCF)
Description: The Survey of Consumer Finances (SCF) is normally a triennial cross-sectional survey of U.S. families. The survey data include information on families’ balance sheets, pensions, income, and demographic characteristics. Information is also included from related surveys of pension providers and the earlier such surveys conducted by the Federal Reserve Board. No other study for the country collects comparable information. Data from the SCF are widely used, from analysis at the Federal Reserve and other branches of government to scholarly work at the major economic research centers.

Return a complete report on everything that a preservationist, data librarian, data scientist, or policy activist might want to know about this data.
prompts.assessment:
# Dataset risk assessment
I would like your help in assessing the likelihood that this data will be changed or removed from its primary location, and that users will no longer be able to access accurate and reliable copies of it, based on the rubric below.

## Sources for context
To help assess the rubric categories, perform additional research on the data, the agency, the data's topics and typical users, covering topics such as proposed regulatory or funding changes, recent news, and political commentary. Use whatever resources you find useful, including the Federal Register (https://www.federalregister.gov) and the federal staffing tracker at https://usajobs-tracker.abigailhaddad.com.

## Rubric
This rubric is divided up into categories. Each category is divided up into risk levels. In your output, please select the appropriate risk level for each category based on your research.

### Historical Data Availability
- Gone: Data files prior to the current year or cycle are no longer publicly available.
- High Risk: Some data files prior to the current year or cycle are removed.
- Moderate Risk: Some data elements that exist in the dataset prior to the current year or cycle are removed.
- No Known Issue: Data prior to the current year or cycle remain accessible with no known alterations.

### Future Data Availability
- Gone: Data collection and publication has been terminated.
- High Risk: Statutory publication deadline missed and/or collection or publication skipped and/or ICR expired for more than one year.
- Moderate Risk: Typical or intended publication date missed and/or collection or publication delayed; ICR expired up to one year.
- No Known Issue: Data published on time or as expected and ICR active or renewed before expiration.

### Data Quality
- Gone: Data collection and publication has been terminated.
- High Risk: Reductions in granularity, timeliness, or frequency.
- Moderate Risk: Potential or emerging risk to granularity, timeliness, or frequency.
- No Known Issue: Maintained or improved granularity, timeliness, or frequency.

### Statutory Context
- Gone: N/A
- High Risk: Statutory authorization is vague and/or there are alternative data collections that could serve as substitutes and/or no known programmatic use.
- Moderate Risk: Not explicitly required by statute but required for the implementation of a state or federal program, and there are no alternative data collections that could serve as substitutes.
- No Known Issue: Statutorily required and/or statutory authorization is explicitly named and it is clear what has to be collected, and there aren't alternative data collections that could serve as substitutes and/or required for implementation of a federal program.

### Staffing and Funding
- Gone: All of the staff in the division or agency are gone and/or all funding has been terminated.
- High Risk: 40% or more of staff lost, and/or 1,000 or more staff lost, and/or budget cut by 20% or more, and/or leadership removed.
- Moderate Risk: 10–39% of staff lost, and/or 500–999 staff lost, and/or budget cut by 10–19%, and/or threatened change in leadership.
- No Known Issue: Less than 10% of staff lost and less than 10% of budget cut and no known change in leadership.

### Policy
- Gone: Data collection and publication has been terminated.
- High Risk: Presidential Action-driven information collection request (ICR); negative policy note on site; other significant changes in accordance with Administration priorities.
- Moderate Risk: Proposed or pending changes; statements by administration officials suggesting a change is being considered or planned.
- No Known Issue: No notable changes since January 2025 affecting what data is collected and published.

For each category, concisely list the evidence and supporting sources that would support each risk level. Then indicate which risk level you find most appropriate and why.

Conclude with a simple summary of risk levels:
Historical Data Availability: <level>
Future Data Availability: <level>
Data Quality: <level>
Statutory Context: <level>
Staffing and Funding: <level>
Policy: <level>

messages.content:
#data research
I am researching a federal dataset. Find out everything you can about this dataset, such as who publishes it, under what authority or mandate, its history, its typical users, and its benefits to the public. Be sure your research comprehensively covers each of those perspectives, as well as any others that you discover or seem useful. I believe this is accurate information, but please check:

Dataset title: Survey of Consumer Finances (SCF)
Description: The Survey of Consumer Finances (SCF) is normally a triennial cross-sectional survey of U.S. families. The survey data include information on families’ balance sheets, pensions, income, and demographic characteristics. Information is also included from related surveys of pension providers and the earlier such surveys conducted by the Federal Reserve Board. No other study for the country collects comparable information. Data from the SCF are widely used, from analysis at the Federal Reserve and other branches of government to scholarly work at the major economic research centers.

Return a complete report on everything that a preservationist, data librarian, data scientist, or policy activist might want to know about this data.

I checked your description and it is accurate. It is copied word for word from the Federal Reserve Board's own "About the SCF" page (federalreserve.gov/econres/aboutscf.htm), so it is the publisher's official summary. A few details need context, covered in section 2.

---

# Survey of Consumer Finances (SCF): research report

## 1. Quick facts

| Item | Detail |
|---|---|
| **Publisher / sponsor** | Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System (Division of Research & Statistics), in cooperation with the U.S. Department of the Treasury |
| **Data collector** | NORC at the University of Chicago, since 1992. Earlier modern waves (1983–89) were run with the University of Michigan's Survey Research Center. |
| **Tax-data partner** | IRS Statistics of Income (SOI) Division, which supplies the frame for the wealthy oversample |
| **OMB control number** | 7100-0287. Fed form number **FR 3059**. Current approval expires **August 31, 2027**. |
| **Frequency** | Every three years. Modern series: 1983, 1986 (re-interview), 1989, 1992 … 2019, 2022, 2025 |
| **Unit of observation** | The "primary economic unit" (family) within a household |
| **Latest released wave** | 2022 (data posted October 18, 2023) |
| **Next wave** | 2025 SCF. Fieldwork began March 2025; summary results expected **late 2026** |
| **Participation** | Voluntary |
| **Access** | Free public microdata on federalreserve.gov. Restricted data through the Standard Application Process (SAP). |
| **Landing page** | https://www.federalreserve.gov/econres/scfindex.htm |

## 2. Checking your description

- **"Normally a triennial cross-sectional survey"**: Correct. "Normally" covers exceptions: the 1986 wave was a re-interview of 1983 respondents, there was a 1983–89 panel, and the Fed re-interviewed 2007 respondents in 2009 to measure the Great Recession.
- **"Related surveys of pension providers"**: Correct, but mainly historical. The Fed's archive page lists a **1983 Survey of Pension Providers** alongside the 1983 SCF. It is not a regular part of current waves.
- **"Earlier such surveys"**: These are the **1962 Survey of Financial Characteristics of Consumers (SFCC)** and the **1963 Survey of Changes in Family Finances (SCFF)**. The Fed calls them "the most direct precursors of the SCF."
- **"No other study … collects comparable information"**: This is the Fed's own wording. The OMB supporting statement calls the SCF "the only source of representative information on the structure of U.S. families' finances." The claim rests mainly on the IRS-based oversample of wealthy families. Other surveys (PSID, SIPP, CPS) measure wealth but miss the very top of the distribution.
- **Start date**: Sources differ slightly. The Fed says the current survey has run every three years since 1983. The 2022 Bulletin says the "modern version" dates from 1989, when the sample design and weights became consistent. Use 1989 as the starting point for strict trend comparisons.

## 3. Legal authority and mandate

- **Statutory basis**: The Fed's Legal Division cites **Sections 2A and 12A of the Federal Reserve Act (12 U.S.C. §225a and §263)**.
  - §2A sets the monetary-policy goals: maximum employment, stable prices and moderate long-term interest rates.
  - §12A governs open market operations "with regard to their bearing upon the general credit situation of the country."
  - The Board and the FOMC say they use the SCF to help meet these obligations. **No law specifically requires the SCF to exist.** It is a discretionary collection justified under the Fed's general monetary-policy mandate. That matters for anyone worried about its long-term survival.
- **Paperwork Reduction Act**: Each wave goes through OMB clearance under authority OMB has delegated to the Board, with public comment notices in the Federal Register. For the 2025 wave, the initial notice was 89 FR 16571 (March 7, 2024) and the final notice was 89 FR 61423 (July 31, 2024). **No public comments were received.**
- **Confidentiality**:
  - Data are collected solely for statistical purposes under a pledge of confidentiality, protected by **CIPSEA** (the Confidential Information Protection and Statistical Efficiency Act, 2018 version). Violations are a felony.
  - Identifying information is exempt from FOIA under exemption 6, and earlier statements also cite (b)(3) through CIPSEA.
  - Duties are split by design: NORC knows respondents' names but never sees the tax-derived income data; the Fed never sees names; SOI never receives survey responses. NORC must destroy identifying information when the study ends.

## 4. History

| Period | Milestone |
|---|---|
| **1946–1971** | The original "Surveys of Consumer Finances" ran every year, sponsored by the Fed and carried out by Michigan's Survey Research Center (Economic Behavior Program). The interviewing unit changed from "spending unit" to "family" in 1964. Archived at ICPSR (Series 55). |
| **Mid-1950s** | A Fed committee on saving statistics, set up at the request of Congress's Joint Committee on the Economic Report, recommended oversampling the wealthy. |
| **1962–63** | SFCC/SCFF, designed with the Census Bureau and the first to oversample wealthy households deliberately. Led by Dorothy Projector (Projector & Weiss, 1966). Data and questionnaires are still on the Fed site, including the earliest surviving un-imputed 1962 file. |
| **1977** | A Survey of Consumer Credit fills the gap and is often counted in the series. |
| **1983** | The modern SCF begins, co-sponsored by **seven federal agencies** in response to financial deregulation and new products such as money market funds. The IRS-based list sample is introduced. |
| **1986, 1983–89** | Re-interview and panel components. |
| **1989–present** | Every three years with a largely stable design. NORC takes over in 1992. |
| **2007–09** | Panel re-interview to capture the Great Recession. |
| **2019** | The Fed launches the **Distributional Financial Accounts (DFA)**, quarterly wealth distributions built by combining the SCF with the Financial Accounts of the U.S. (Z.1). |
| **2022** | The area sample is redesigned to oversample households predicted to be Black, Hispanic or Asian, at about 50% higher sampling rates. |
| **2025** | Fieldwork: up to 7,000 interviews averaging about 110 minutes, by phone or in person. A letter from Chair Powell went to about 13,000 households, sampled from 119 geographic areas. |

## 5. Method (for data scientists)

- **Two-part sample**:
  1. A multistage area-probability sample, which covers widely held items such as homes, cars and checking accounts.
  2. A list sample drawn from the IRS SOI Individual Research Tax File, which oversamples the wealthy (see Bricker, Henriques & Moore, FEDS 2017-114).
  - **People on the Forbes 400 list are excluded** from sampling.
- **2022 sample**: 4,602 completed interviews (3,298 area sample, 1,304 list sample), representing 131.3 million households. In 2019 there were 5,783 interviews (4,291 area, 1,492 list).
- **Response rates**: Just over 40% in the 2022 area sample and about one-third in the list sample. Among the wealthiest list strata it was roughly half that. The Fed notes refusal is strongly correlated with wealth, and the list sample lets it adjust for this, which other surveys cannot do.
- **Missing data are multiply imputed**: each family appears as **five implicates**, so 4,602 families yield 23,010 records. **Do not treat the rows as independent observations.** Estimates must be combined across implicates using Rubin's rules.
- **Weights**:
  - Use main weight X42001, which is adjusted for nonresponse and calibrated to Current Population Survey totals. A consistent-weight series (X42000) is provided for trends since 1989.
  - Standard errors require the **replicate weight file**, which is posted separately. Unweighted analysis is badly biased because of the wealthy oversample.
- **Disclosure avoidance**: The public data are deliberately altered (rounding, top-coding, swapping and similar steps). Seven 2022 cases were dropped entirely, leaving 22,975 public records for 4,595 families. The codebook describes the steps.
- **Files and formats**:
  - The full public dataset (thousands of variables) comes as SAS (CPORT and COPY/EXPORT), Stata and ASCII, with Excel or tab-delimited variable maps.
  - A **summary extract** has the Bulletin's derived variables (net worth, asset categories, etc.).
  - The codebook is a large ASCII text file and includes the SAS code used to build the summary variables.
  - Historical tables, an interactive chartbook, and standard-error documentation are also posted.
  - The community-maintained "asdfree" R guides show how to analyze the survey in R.
- **Content areas**: assets (financial, housing, real estate, businesses, vehicles), debts (mortgages, credit cards, student and auto loans), income, pensions and retirement accounts, work history, use of financial institutions, inheritances and giving, attitudes and expectations, demographics and health, and since 2022 COVID-19 impacts.

## 6. Typical users

- **Federal Reserve**: monetary policy and financial stability analysis, the DFA, FEDS working papers and the Federal Reserve Bulletin.
- **Other government bodies**: Treasury (Office of Tax Analysis), CBO's wealth-distribution reports, the Joint Committee on Taxation, Commerce, FDIC, CFPB, SSA and GAO. NORC also cites consumer protection initiatives and federal legislation.
- **Academics**: wealth inequality, saving and retirement adequacy, household finance and portfolio choice, the racial wealth gap, student debt, small-business ownership, and the debate over how concentrated top wealth is (for example Saez–Zucman versus Bricker et al.).
- **Think tanks and advocacy groups**: Urban Institute, Brookings, Pew, Center for American Progress, AEI, St. Louis Fed's Institute for Economic Equity (formerly the Center for Household Financial Stability), and Institute for Policy Studies.
- **Journalists, financial planners and industry**: benchmarks such as "median net worth by age."

## 7. Benefits to the public

- It provides the authoritative U.S. figures for household **net worth and its distribution**. In 2022, real median net worth was $192,900 (up 37% from 2019, the largest three-year rise in the modern SCF), and real mean net worth was $1,063,700.
- It has the most reliable **racial and ethnic wealth-gap** statistics, strengthened by the 2022 oversample. Black families' median net worth was $44,900 in 2022.
- It shows how economic shocks spread across households, including the Great Recession, the pandemic and housing booms.
- It supports evidence for policy on taxes such as wealth or estate taxes, retirement policy, consumer credit, student debt and financial inclusion.
- It is free and openly downloadable, with 60 years of comparable precursors.

## 8. Limitations and criticisms

- The **Forbes 400 exclusion** and the limited ability to capture extreme wealth mean top shares are understated unless adjusted. Researchers often add Forbes data back in.
- **Low response rates**, though the oversample and weights compensate.
- **Small sample** (about 4,600–6,000 families), so there are **no reliable state or local estimates** and subgroups are thin.
- Only every **three years** and cross-sectional; the DFA partly fills the gap between waves.
- Public data are altered for privacy; the 2022 race oversample and similar changes affect comparisons over time; and topics change between waves.
- No specific statutory mandate, so continuation depends on the Fed's discretion and budget.

## 9. Preservation and data-librarian notes

- **Where copies live**:
  - Current and past waves (1983 onward, including the 1983–89 panel, the 2007–09 panel and the pension provider survey) are on federalreserve.gov ("Previous Surveys").
  - 1962/63 data are at /econres/scf_6263.htm.
  - The 1946–71 annual surveys are at **ICPSR Series 55**.
  - Federal Reserve Bulletin articles and press releases are archived on **FRASER** (St. Louis Fed).
  - OMB supporting statements are on reginfo.gov and omb.report.
- **Risks**:
  - The Fed revises files after release, for example re-weighting or updating the consistent weight series and inflation adjustments. Record the "Last Updated" dates (2022 files: 10/18/2023) and keep superseded versions.
  - The SAS CPORT and transport formats are a long-term format-obsolescence risk. Keep the ASCII and Stata versions too.
  - Keep the codebook, the replicate weights and the summary-variable SAS macros with the data, because the data cannot be used properly without them.
- **Related but separate Fed products**: the Distributional Financial Accounts, the Survey of Household Economics and Decisionmaking (SHED), the Survey of Consumer Expectations (New York Fed), and Michigan's Surveys of Consumers. The last shares the old name lineage but is now a different sentiment survey.
- **Watch for**: the 2025 SCF release, expected in late 2026. The press release says interviews would run through December 2025, while the OMB filing allows fieldwork through March 2026. I could not confirm whether the 2025 results are out yet. After that, watch for OMB renewal before the August 2027 expiration, which is needed for a 2028 wave.

## 10. Key sources

- Fed SCF landing page and About page: federalreserve.gov/econres/scfindex.htm, /aboutscf.htm
- 2022 codebook: federalreserve.gov/econres/files/codebk2022.txt
- "Changes in U.S. Family Finances from 2019 to 2022," Federal Reserve Bulletin, October 2023 (scf23.pdf)
- OMB supporting statements A and B, FR 3059 (ICR 202408-7100-005)
- Fed press release of February 28, 2025, and the participant page federalreserve.gov/scf
- NORC SCF project page; ICPSR Series 55; Projector & Weiss (1966)
